chapter_text:
CHAPTER 25 - HEREDITY

Introduction

Why do children resemble their parents? Why is a kitten always a cat and never a dog? Living things produce offspring of their own kind, and those offspring carry a mixture of features from their parents. The branch of biology that studies how characters (traits) are passed from one generation to the next is called GENETICS, and the actual transmission of characters from parents to offspring is called HEREDITY. Alongside the similarities, there are always small differences between parents and offspring, and among offspring themselves; these differences are called VARIATIONS. Heredity and variation together shape the living world and supply the raw material for evolution.

25.1 HEREDITY AND VARIATION

HEREDITY is the transmission of characters (features such as eye colour, height, flower colour, seed shape) from parents to their offspring through the reproductive cells (gametes). Because of heredity, offspring resemble their parents and belong to the same species.
VARIATION refers to the differences found among individuals of the same species. Two kinds are recognised. (a) Inheritable (genetic) variation is caused by changes in the genes or chromosomes and is passed on to the next generation. (b) Non-inheritable (somatic/acquired) variation is caused by the environment - food, climate, exercise, accident - affects only the body cells, and is NOT passed on.
Variations are useful: they make a population diverse, help species survive changing conditions, and provide the raw material on which natural selection acts during evolution.

25.2 GREGOR MENDEL AND HIS EXPERIMENTS

The systematic study of heredity began with GREGOR JOHANN MENDEL (1822-1884), an Austrian monk who worked in the garden of his monastery at Brunn. Between 1856 and 1863 he carried out careful breeding experiments on the GARDEN PEA (Pisum sativum) and worked out the basic laws of inheritance. He is rightly called the 'Father of Genetics'.
Mendel chose the garden pea for several good reasons:
 - It is easy to grow and has a short life cycle, so many generations can be raised quickly.
 - It has several clearly contrasting characters (for example tall vs dwarf plants, round vs wrinkled seeds, green vs yellow seeds, violet vs white flowers).
 - Its flowers are normally SELF-POLLINATING (bisexual flowers that fertilise themselves), which keeps a variety pure; but Mendel could also CROSS-POLLINATE two plants by hand when he wished.
 - It produces a large number of offspring, allowing reliable counting and ratios.
Mendel first produced PURE-BREEDING (true-breeding) lines by self-pollinating for several generations. Then he crossed plants differing in a single character and counted the offspring carefully over two or three generations - a quantitative approach that was new for his time.

25.3 IMPORTANT TERMS

To follow Mendel's work we need a set of terms:
 - GENE: a unit of heredity; a segment of DNA that carries the instruction for a particular character.
 - ALLELE: one of the alternative forms of a gene. For plant height the gene has a tall allele (T) and a dwarf allele (t).
 - GENOTYPE: the genetic make-up of an organism, written as the pair of alleles, e.g. TT, Tt or tt.
 - PHENOTYPE: the observable character that results from the genotype, e.g. tall or dwarf.
 - DOMINANT allele: the allele that expresses itself in the phenotype even when present in a single copy (T, tall). It is written with a capital letter.
 - RECESSIVE allele: the allele that is expressed only when present in a double copy, i.e. when the dominant allele is absent (t, dwarf). It is written with a small letter.
 - HOMOZYGOUS: having two identical alleles for a character (TT or tt); also called pure.
 - HETEROZYGOUS: having two different alleles for a character (Tt); also called hybrid.

25.4 MONOHYBRID CROSS AND THE LAWS OF INHERITANCE

A MONOHYBRID CROSS follows the inheritance of a SINGLE pair of contrasting characters. Mendel crossed a pure tall pea plant (TT) with a pure dwarf plant (tt). The parents are the P (parental) generation.
F1 generation: All the offspring were TALL (Tt). The dwarf character disappeared. The tall allele (T) masked the dwarf allele (t).
F2 generation: When the F1 tall plants (Tt) were self-pollinated (Tt x Tt), BOTH tall and dwarf plants reappeared in a ratio of about 3 TALL : 1 DWARF. The hidden dwarf character had returned.
The cross can be shown in a PUNNETT SQUARE. The Tt parent makes gametes T and t; so does the other Tt parent. Combining them:
        T        t
   T    TT       Tt
   t    Tt       tt
The four boxes give genotypes TT : Tt : Tt : tt, i.e. a genotypic ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Since TT and Tt are both tall and only tt is dwarf, the PHENOTYPIC ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

From such crosses Mendel framed two laws (for a single character):
 - LAW OF DOMINANCE: When two organisms with a contrasting pair of characters are crossed, only one character (the dominant one) appears in the F1; the other (the recessive) remains hidden.
 - LAW OF SEGREGATION (Law of Purity of Gametes): The two alleles of a character separate (segregate) during the formation of gametes, so that each gamete carries only ONE allele of the pair. The alleles come together again at fertilisation. This is why the recessive character reappears in the F2.

25.5 DIHYBRID CROSS AND INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT

A DIHYBRID CROSS follows TWO pairs of characters at the same time. Mendel crossed pure plants with round-yellow seeds (RRYY) and pure plants with wrinkled-green seeds (rryy). The F1 were all round-yellow (RrYy), confirming that round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) over green (y).
When the F1 (RrYy) were self-pollinated, the F2 showed FOUR phenotypes in the ratio:
   9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green
i.e. a 9:3:3:1 ratio. Importantly, new combinations (round-green and wrinkled-yellow) appeared that were not present in the parents. This led Mendel to the:
 - LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT: When two pairs of characters are inherited together, each pair assorts (is distributed to the gametes) INDEPENDENTLY of the other. The inheritance of seed shape does not affect the inheritance of seed colour.

25.6 CHROMOSOMES, DNA AND GENES

Mendel did not know about chromosomes; their link to heredity came later. Inside the nucleus of every cell are thread-like structures called CHROMOSOMES, made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) wound with proteins. DNA is a long double-stranded molecule shaped like a twisted ladder (the DOUBLE HELIX). A GENE is a particular segment of DNA that codes for a character. Chromosomes therefore carry the genes, and genes are the physical basis of Mendel's 'factors'.
Chromosomes occur in PAIRS in body cells. Humans have 23 pairs (46 chromosomes in all): 22 pairs of ordinary chromosomes called AUTOSOMES and 1 pair of SEX CHROMOSOMES. The two members of a pair carry genes for the same characters at the same positions - so each character is represented by a pair of alleles, exactly as Mendel deduced. During gamete formation the pairs separate (segregation), and gametes have HALF the number of chromosomes (23 in humans); the full number is restored at fertilisation.

25.7 SEX DETERMINATION IN HUMANS

The sex of a child is decided by the SEX CHROMOSOMES. In humans the female has two X chromosomes (XX) and the male has one X and one Y chromosome (XY).
A mother (XX) produces eggs that all carry an X chromosome. A father (XY) produces two kinds of sperm: half carry X and half carry Y. At fertilisation:
 - X (egg) + X (sperm) -> XX -> a GIRL.
 - X (egg) + Y (sperm) -> XY -> a BOY.
Because the sperm decides whether the embryo receives an X or a Y, it is the FATHER who determines the sex of the child, not the mother. On average half the children are girls and half are boys (1:1 ratio).

25.8 SEX-LINKED INHERITANCE

Some genes are located on the sex chromosomes - especially the X chromosome - and the characters they control are said to be SEX-LINKED. Because a male has only one X chromosome, a recessive allele on his single X is expressed directly (there is no second X to mask it). This is why disorders such as COLOUR BLINDNESS and HAEMOPHILIA are far more common in males than in females. A female, with two X chromosomes, usually needs the recessive allele on BOTH X chromosomes to show the disorder; with one copy she is a healthy CARRIER.

25.9 ACQUIRED AND INHERITED TRAITS; LINK TO EVOLUTION

It is important to distinguish two kinds of traits. INHERITED (inborn) traits arise from genes and are passed to the offspring - eye colour, blood group, flower colour. ACQUIRED traits develop during an individual's lifetime due to use, environment or training - the big muscles of a wrestler, a learned language, a scar. Acquired traits affect only the body (somatic) cells, NOT the reproductive cells, so they are NOT inherited. (Lamarck's old idea that acquired characters are inherited has been rejected.)
Inheritable variations are the link to EVOLUTION. Small genetic differences make individuals of a population slightly different. Those variations that suit the environment help an organism survive and reproduce better; over many generations such useful variations accumulate and new forms (and eventually new species) arise. Thus variation is the RAW MATERIAL of evolution, and heredity is the machinery that carries it forward.

25.10 GENETIC DISORDERS - A BRIEF NOTE

When genes or chromosomes carry errors, the result can be a GENETIC DISORDER. A few examples: COLOUR BLINDNESS and HAEMOPHILIA (X-linked recessive disorders, commoner in males); SICKLE-CELL ANAEMIA and THALASSAEMIA (disorders of the blood caused by faulty genes); and DOWN SYNDROME (caused by an extra chromosome 21). Such disorders show that heredity is governed by genes and chromosomes that must be transmitted accurately from one generation to the next.

SUMMARY

 - Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring; variation is the differences among individuals. Inheritable variation is the raw material of evolution.
 - Gregor Mendel, the Father of Genetics, used the garden pea (easy to grow, contrasting characters, self- or cross-pollination, many offspring) to discover the laws of inheritance.
 - Key terms: gene, allele, genotype (TT/Tt/tt), phenotype, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous.
 - Monohybrid cross (TT x tt): F1 all tall (Tt); F2 = 3 tall : 1 dwarf (genotype 1:2:1). This gives the Law of Dominance and the Law of Segregation.
 - Dihybrid cross (RRYY x rryy): F2 = 9:3:3:1, giving the Law of Independent Assortment.
 - Chromosomes (in pairs) are made of DNA; a gene is a DNA segment. Humans have 23 pairs (22 autosome pairs + 1 sex-chromosome pair).
 - Sex determination: female XX, male XY; the father's sperm (X or Y) decides the sex of the child.
 - Acquired traits are not inherited; only genetic (inherited) traits pass to the next generation.

chapter_summary.title: Heredity - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 25 explains heredity and variation, Mendel's experiments on the garden pea, the monohybrid (3:1) and dihybrid (9:3:3:1) crosses with his laws of inheritance, chromosomes/DNA/genes, and how sex is determined in humans.

sections.heading: Heredity and variation
bullets: Heredity is the transmission of characters (traits) from parents to offspring through the gametes; it is why offspring resemble their parents.
Variation is the differences among individuals of the same species. Inheritable (genetic) variation is passed on; non-inheritable (acquired/environmental) variation is not.
Inheritable variation makes a population diverse and is the raw material on which natural selection acts during evolution.

sections.heading: Mendel and key terms
bullets: Gregor Mendel (Father of Genetics) used the garden pea because it grows fast, has clear contrasting characters, can be self- or cross-pollinated, and gives many offspring.
Gene = unit of heredity (segment of DNA); allele = an alternative form of a gene (T or t).
Genotype = genetic make-up (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype = observable trait (tall, dwarf).
Dominant allele shows in a single copy (T); recessive shows only in double copy (tt). Homozygous = two identical alleles; heterozygous = two different alleles.

sections.heading: Monohybrid cross and laws
bullets: Monohybrid cross follows one character. TT x tt gives an F1 that is all tall (Tt) - the dwarf trait is hidden.
Selfing the F1 (Tt x Tt) gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of 3 tall : 1 dwarf and a genotypic ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.
Law of Dominance: only the dominant character appears in the F1.
Law of Segregation: the two alleles of a character separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele.

sections.heading: Dihybrid cross and independent assortment
bullets: A dihybrid cross follows two characters together. RRYY x rryy gives an F1 that is all round-yellow (RrYy).
Selfing the F1 gives an F2 ratio of 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green (9:3:3:1).
New combinations (round-green, wrinkled-yellow) appear, showing the two characters are inherited independently.
Law of Independent Assortment: each pair of characters assorts into the gametes independently of the other pair.

sections.heading: Chromosomes, genes and sex determination
bullets: Chromosomes in the nucleus are made of DNA (a double helix); a gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a character.
Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in all): 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
Females are XX and males are XY. The mother gives only X; the father gives X or Y, so the father determines the sex of the child.
Sex-linked recessive disorders (colour blindness, haemophilia) are commoner in males because they have only one X chromosome.

key_takeaways: Heredity transmits characters from parents to offspring; inheritable variation is the raw material of evolution.
Mendel, the Father of Genetics, used the garden pea to discover the laws of inheritance.
Key terms: gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous.
Monohybrid cross: F1 all dominant; F2 = 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic (Law of Dominance, Law of Segregation).
Dihybrid cross F2 = 9:3:3:1, giving the Law of Independent Assortment.
Chromosomes are made of DNA and carry genes; humans have 23 pairs (22 autosomes + 1 sex pair).
Sex is determined by sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male); the father's sperm decides the child's sex.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Heredity (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-25 for Lesson 25 (Heredity). Attempt all questions. Use Punnett squares where a genetics problem is given and show the genotype and phenotype ratios clearly.

questions.question: Define heredity and variation. Give one example of each.
questions.answer: HEREDITY is the transmission of characters (traits) from parents to their offspring through the gametes - for example, a child inheriting the eye colour of a parent. VARIATION is the differences found among individuals of the same species - for example, differences in height among children of the same parents.
questions.explanation: Heredity = transmission of traits; variation = differences among individuals.

questions.question: Give three reasons why Mendel chose the garden pea (Pisum sativum) for his experiments.
questions.answer: (1) It is easy to grow and has a short life cycle, so many generations can be raised quickly. (2) It shows several clearly contrasting characters (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds, etc.). (3) It is normally self-pollinating (keeping lines pure) but can also be cross-pollinated by hand, and it produces many offspring for reliable counting.
questions.explanation: Fast growth, contrasting traits, self/cross pollination, many offspring.

questions.question: Distinguish between genotype and phenotype with an example.
questions.answer: GENOTYPE is the genetic make-up of an organism, written as the pair of alleles, e.g. TT, Tt or tt. PHENOTYPE is the observable character that results, e.g. tall or dwarf. Example: both TT and Tt plants have the SAME phenotype (tall) but DIFFERENT genotypes; only tt is dwarf.
questions.explanation: Genotype = allele pair; phenotype = visible trait.

questions.question: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). Draw the Punnett square for the F2 generation (selfing the F1) and state the genotypic and phenotypic ratios.
questions.answer:
P: TT x tt -> F1 all Tt (tall). Selfing F1: Tt x Tt. Each parent gives gametes T and t.
Punnett square:
        T        t
   T    TT       Tt
   t    Tt       tt
Genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt = genotypic ratio 1:2:1. Phenotypes: TT and Tt are tall, tt is dwarf, so 3 tall : 1 dwarf = phenotypic ratio 3:1.

questions.question: State Mendel's Law of Dominance and Law of Segregation.
questions.answer: LAW OF DOMINANCE: when two organisms with a contrasting pair of characters are crossed, only the dominant character appears in the F1; the recessive remains hidden. LAW OF SEGREGATION (purity of gametes): the two alleles of a character separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele of the pair; they reunite at fertilisation.
questions.explanation: Dominance = only dominant shows in F1; Segregation = alleles separate into gametes.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross RrYy x RrYy, what is the F2 phenotypic ratio and what law does it illustrate?
questions.answer: The F2 phenotypic ratio is 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green, i.e. 9:3:3:1. It illustrates the LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT: each pair of characters (seed shape and seed colour) is inherited independently of the other.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a chromosome, DNA and a gene? How many chromosomes do humans have?
questions.answer: A CHROMOSOME is a thread-like structure in the nucleus made of DNA wound with proteins. DNA is a long double-stranded molecule (a double helix). A GENE is a particular segment of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a character. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in all): 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Chromosome carries DNA; gene = DNA segment; humans 23 pairs.

questions.question: Explain why it is the father, not the mother, who determines the sex of a child.
questions.answer: The mother is XX and produces eggs that all carry an X chromosome. The father is XY and produces two kinds of sperm: half carry X and half carry Y. If an X-sperm fertilises the egg, the child is XX (girl); if a Y-sperm fertilises it, the child is XY (boy). Since the sperm supplies either X or Y, the father determines the sex of the child.
questions.explanation: Father supplies X or Y; mother only X.

questions.question: Distinguish between inherited (inborn) and acquired traits with one example each. Are acquired traits inherited?
questions.answer: INHERITED traits come from genes and pass to the offspring, e.g. blood group or eye colour. ACQUIRED traits develop during an individual's lifetime due to environment or use, e.g. the big muscles of a wrestler or a learned language. Acquired traits affect only body (somatic) cells, not the gametes, so they are NOT inherited.
questions.explanation: Inherited = genetic, passed on; acquired = lifetime, not passed on.

questions.question: What is meant by sex-linked inheritance? Why are colour blindness and haemophilia more common in men than in women?
questions.answer: Sex-linked inheritance is the inheritance of characters controlled by genes located on the sex chromosomes, especially the X chromosome. Colour blindness and haemophilia are caused by recessive alleles on the X chromosome. A male has only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on it is expressed directly (there is no second X to mask it). A female has two X chromosomes, so she usually needs the recessive allele on BOTH X chromosomes to show the disorder; with one copy she is a healthy carrier. Therefore these disorders are far more common in men than in women.
questions.explanation: Males have one X, so recessive X-linked alleles show directly.

A segment of DNA that codes for a character is called a ____.
In humans, a female has the sex chromosomes ____.
Colour blindness and haemophilia are examples of ____ inheritance.
Define heredity.
questions.answer: Heredity is the transmission of characters (traits) from parents to their offspring through the reproductive cells (gametes). Because of heredity, offspring resemble their parents and belong to the same species.

questions.question: What is variation? Name its two types.
questions.answer: Variation is the differences found among individuals of the same species. The two types are (1) inheritable (genetic) variation, caused by changes in genes/chromosomes and passed on, and (2) non-inheritable (acquired) variation, caused by the environment and not passed on.
questions.explanation: Differences among individuals; inheritable and acquired.

questions.question: Why is inheritable variation important for a species?
questions.answer: Inheritable variation makes the individuals of a population genetically different from one another. This diversity helps some individuals survive changes in the environment (disease, climate, food). Such useful variations are passed on and accumulate over generations, providing the raw material on which natural selection acts during evolution. Without variation a population could not adapt or evolve.
questions.explanation: Diversity aids survival and is raw material of evolution.

questions.question: Why are acquired traits not inherited?
questions.answer: Acquired traits develop during an individual's lifetime due to environment, use or training (e.g. a wrestler's muscles). They affect only the body (somatic) cells and do not change the genes in the reproductive cells (gametes). Since only the gametes pass to the next generation, acquired traits are not inherited.
questions.explanation: They do not change the gametes.

questions.question: Who was Gregor Mendel and what is he famous for?
questions.answer: Gregor Johann Mendel (1822-1884) was an Austrian monk who carried out breeding experiments on the garden pea in his monastery garden. He worked out the basic laws of inheritance and is called the Father of Genetics.

questions.question: List the features of the garden pea that made it suitable for Mendel's experiments.
questions.answer: (1) Easy to grow with a short life cycle, so many generations can be raised quickly. (2) Several clearly contrasting characters (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled, etc.). (3) Normally self-pollinating, keeping varieties pure, but can be cross-pollinated by hand. (4) Produces many offspring, allowing reliable counting and ratios.
questions.explanation: Fast growth, contrasting traits, self/cross pollination, many offspring.

questions.question: What is a pure-breeding (true-breeding) line and how did Mendel obtain it?
questions.answer: A pure-breeding line is a homozygous line that always produces offspring like itself when self-pollinated. Mendel obtained such lines by self-pollinating pea plants for several generations until each line bred true for a chosen character (e.g. always tall or always dwarf).
questions.explanation: Homozygous lines obtained by repeated self-pollination.

questions.question: Define gene and allele.
questions.answer: A GENE is a unit of heredity - a segment of DNA that carries the instruction for a particular character. An ALLELE is one of the alternative forms of a gene, for example T (tall) and t (dwarf) for plant height.
questions.explanation: Gene = unit of heredity; allele = its alternative form.

questions.question: Differentiate between dominant and recessive alleles.
questions.answer: A DOMINANT allele expresses itself in the phenotype even when present in a single copy and is written with a capital letter (T). A RECESSIVE allele is expressed only when present in a double copy (homozygous, tt) and is written with a small letter; otherwise it is masked by the dominant allele.
questions.explanation: Dominant shows in single copy; recessive needs double copy.

questions.question: Differentiate between homozygous and heterozygous with examples.
questions.answer: A HOMOZYGOUS organism has two identical alleles for a character (TT or tt) and is also called pure. A HETEROZYGOUS organism has two different alleles (Tt) and is also called hybrid. Example: TT and tt are homozygous, Tt is heterozygous.
questions.explanation: Homozygous = same alleles; heterozygous = different alleles.

questions.question: A tall pea plant is crossed with a dwarf plant and all offspring are tall. What does this tell you about the genotype of the tall parent?
questions.answer: Since all the offspring are tall and none is dwarf, the tall parent must be homozygous (pure tall, TT). If it had been Tt, half the offspring would have been dwarf when crossed with a dwarf (tt). Therefore the tall parent is TT.
questions.explanation: All tall offspring implies TT tall parent.

questions.question: What is a monohybrid cross?
questions.answer: A monohybrid cross is a cross that follows the inheritance of a single pair of contrasting characters, for example tall versus dwarf in pea plants (TT x tt).

questions.question: In a monohybrid cross between a pure tall (TT) and a pure dwarf (tt) pea plant, describe the F1 and F2 generations.
questions.answer: P: TT x tt. F1: all the offspring are tall (genotype Tt) - the dwarf character is hidden. F2: when the F1 (Tt) are self-pollinated (Tt x Tt), both tall and dwarf plants reappear in a phenotypic ratio of 3 tall : 1 dwarf, with a genotypic ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

questions.question: Using a Punnett square, find the offspring ratio of the cross Tt x tt.
questions.answer:
Tt makes gametes T and t; tt makes only t.
        t        t
   T    Tt       Tt
   t    tt       tt
Genotypes: 2 Tt : 2 tt = 1:1. Phenotypes: 1 tall (Tt) : 1 dwarf (tt). This is a 1:1 ratio, which is why such a cross (a test cross) reveals a heterozygous parent.
questions.explanation: Tt x tt gives 1 tall : 1 dwarf.

questions.question: In the F2 of a monohybrid cross, out of 400 plants how many would be expected to be dwarf and how many pure tall? Show working.
questions.answer: The F2 ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf, and within the tall the genotype ratio is 1 TT : 2 Tt. Of 400 plants: dwarf (tt) = 1/4 x 400 = 100. Pure tall (TT) = 1/4 x 400 = 100. (The remaining 200 are heterozygous tall, Tt.)

questions.question: What is a Punnett square used for?
questions.answer: A Punnett square is a grid used to predict the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring of a genetic cross. The possible gametes of one parent are written across the top and those of the other parent down the side; combining them fills the boxes with all possible offspring genotypes.
questions.explanation: Grid to predict offspring genotypes and ratios.

questions.question: State Mendel's Law of Dominance.
questions.answer: The Law of Dominance states that when two organisms differing in a contrasting pair of characters are crossed, only one character (the dominant one) appears in the F1 generation, while the other (the recessive) remains hidden.
questions.explanation: Only the dominant character shows in F1.

questions.question: State Mendel's Law of Segregation and explain why it is also called the law of purity of gametes.
questions.answer: The Law of Segregation states that the two alleles of a character separate (segregate) during the formation of gametes, so each gamete receives only ONE allele of the pair. It is called the law of purity of gametes because every gamete carries a single pure allele, never a mixture; the alleles reunite at fertilisation.
questions.explanation: Alleles separate; each gamete is pure for one allele.

questions.question: Why does the recessive character reappear in the F2 generation though it was absent in the F1?
questions.answer: In the F1 (Tt) the recessive allele (t) is present but masked by the dominant allele (T), so the recessive character (dwarf) is hidden, not lost. During gamete formation the alleles segregate (Law of Segregation), so F1 plants produce both T and t gametes. When two t gametes combine in the F2, the homozygous recessive genotype (tt) is formed and the recessive character reappears - in about 1/4 of the F2.
questions.explanation: Hidden t allele in F1 segregates and pairs as tt in F2.

questions.question: What is a dihybrid cross?
questions.answer: A dihybrid cross is a cross that follows two pairs of contrasting characters at the same time, for example seed shape (round/wrinkled) and seed colour (yellow/green) in peas - RRYY x rryy.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross RRYY x rryy, what is the F1 and the F2 phenotypic ratio? What does the result show?
questions.answer: F1: all plants are round-yellow (RrYy), since round (R) and yellow (Y) are dominant. F2 (RrYy x RrYy): four phenotypes appear in the ratio 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green (9:3:3:1). The appearance of new combinations (round-green, wrinkled-yellow) shows that the two characters are inherited independently of each other.
questions.explanation: F1 round-yellow; F2 9:3:3:1; characters assort independently.

questions.question: State Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment.
questions.answer: The Law of Independent Assortment states that when two pairs of characters are inherited together, each pair assorts (is distributed to the gametes) independently of the other. Thus the inheritance of one character (e.g. seed shape) does not affect the inheritance of another (e.g. seed colour).

questions.question: How many kinds of gametes can a plant with the genotype RrYy produce, and what are they?
questions.answer: An RrYy plant can produce 4 kinds of gametes. Because the R/r and Y/y pairs assort independently, the combinations are RY, Ry, rY and ry (each in equal proportion).
questions.explanation: Four gamete types: RY, Ry, rY, ry.

questions.question: What are chromosomes and what are they made of?
questions.answer: Chromosomes are thread-like structures found in the nucleus of a cell. They are made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) wound together with proteins, and they carry the genes that control the characters of an organism.
questions.explanation: Nuclear thread-like structures of DNA and protein.

questions.question: Explain the relationship between chromosomes, DNA and genes.
questions.answer: A chromosome is made of a long molecule of DNA wound with proteins. DNA is a double-stranded molecule shaped like a twisted ladder (double helix). A gene is a particular segment of this DNA that codes for one character. So genes are parts of DNA, and DNA (with protein) makes up chromosomes - chromosomes carry the genes.
questions.explanation: Gene = DNA segment; DNA + protein = chromosome.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are present in human body cells and gametes? Name the two kinds of chromosomes.
questions.answer: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); a gamete (egg or sperm) has 23. The two kinds are AUTOSOMES (22 pairs, controlling body characters) and SEX CHROMOSOMES (1 pair, determining sex).
questions.explanation: Body cell 46, gamete 23; autosomes and sex chromosomes.

questions.question: How is sex determined in humans?
questions.answer: Sex is determined by the sex chromosomes. A female has two X chromosomes (XX) and a male has one X and one Y (XY). When an X-bearing sperm fertilises the egg the child is XX (girl); when a Y-bearing sperm fertilises it, the child is XY (boy).
questions.explanation: XX female, XY male; sperm decides.

questions.question: Using a cross diagram, show why there is an equal chance of having a boy or a girl.
questions.answer:
Mother (XX) gives only X eggs. Father (XY) gives X and Y sperm in equal numbers.
         X(egg)
  X(sperm)  XX -> girl
  Y(sperm)  XY -> boy
Half the sperm carry X (giving XX girls) and half carry Y (giving XY boys), so there is a 1:1 chance - an equal probability of a boy or a girl at each fertilisation.
questions.explanation: Half X sperm, half Y sperm gives 1:1.

questions.question: Why are sex-linked recessive disorders such as colour blindness more common in men than in women?
questions.answer: These disorders are caused by recessive alleles on the X chromosome. A male (XY) has only one X, so a single recessive allele on it is expressed directly because there is no second X to mask it. A female (XX) has two X chromosomes, so she usually needs the recessive allele on BOTH X chromosomes to show the disorder; with one copy she is only a carrier. Hence such disorders appear far more often in men.
questions.explanation: Males have one X, so one recessive X allele shows.

questions.question: Distinguish between autosomes and sex chromosomes.
questions.answer: AUTOSOMES are the chromosomes that control the ordinary body characters; humans have 22 pairs of them. SEX CHROMOSOMES are the one pair that determines the sex of the individual (XX in females, XY in males). Together they make up the 23 pairs in a human cell.
questions.explanation: 22 pairs autosomes (body traits) + 1 pair sex chromosomes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Within a single family, children resemble their parents in many ways, yet no two children are exactly alike. Some differences come from the genes; others, such as a suntan or a learned skill, come from the surroundings and are gained during life.

(i) What name is given to the passing of features from parents to children?
(ii) What name is given to the differences among the children?
(iii) Classify the two types of variation mentioned.
(iv) Which type is important for evolution and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Heredity.
(ii) Variation.
(iii) Two types: inheritable (genetic) variation, caused by changes in genes/chromosomes and passed on; and non-inheritable (acquired) variation, such as a suntan or a learned skill, which is gained during life and not passed on.
(iv) Inheritable variation is important for evolution because it is heritable and provides the raw material on which natural selection acts; useful variations accumulate over generations and lead to new forms.
questions.explanation: Heredity vs variation; inheritable variation drives evolution.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk, experimented on the garden pea between 1856 and 1863. He first created pure lines and then crossed plants differing in single characters, carefully counting the offspring over several generations.

(i) Why is Mendel called the Father of Genetics?
(ii) Give two reasons why the pea was a good choice.
(iii) What is a pure (true-breeding) line?
(iv) Why was counting offspring over generations important?
questions.answer:
(i) Because he was the first to work out the basic laws of inheritance through systematic experiments.
(ii) Any two: it grows fast with a short life cycle; it has clear contrasting characters; it can be self- or cross-pollinated; it gives many offspring.
(iii) A pure (true-breeding) line is a homozygous line that always produces offspring like itself when self-pollinated.
(iv) Counting large numbers of offspring over generations revealed consistent numerical ratios (such as 3:1), which let Mendel deduce the laws of inheritance.
questions.explanation: Mendel's method: pure lines, single-character crosses, counting ratios.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In pea plants the allele for tallness (T) is dominant over the allele for dwarfness (t). A plant may be TT, Tt or tt.

(i) Which plants are tall and which are dwarf?
(ii) Which genotype is heterozygous?
(iii) Define genotype and phenotype.
(iv) Why do TT and Tt plants look the same?
questions.answer:
(i) TT and Tt plants are tall; tt plants are dwarf.
(ii) Tt is the heterozygous genotype.
(iii) Genotype is the genetic make-up (the pair of alleles, e.g. TT/Tt/tt); phenotype is the observable character (tall or dwarf).
(iv) Because T (tall) is dominant, a single T allele is enough to make the plant tall, so both TT and Tt show the tall phenotype even though their genotypes differ.
questions.explanation: Dominant T masks recessive t; same phenotype, different genotype.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). The F1 plants are all tall. They are then self-pollinated to give the F2 generation.

(i) What is the genotype and phenotype of the F1?
(ii) Draw the Punnett square for the F2.
(iii) State the F2 genotypic and phenotypic ratios.
(iv) Which law explains the reappearance of the dwarf plants?
questions.answer:
(i) F1 genotype Tt; phenotype all tall.
(ii) Tt x Tt:
        T        t
   T    TT       Tt
   t    Tt       tt
(iii) Genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt (1:2:1); phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf (3:1).
(iv) The Law of Segregation - the alleles separate into gametes in the F1 and recombine, so tt (dwarf) reappears in the F2.
questions.explanation: F1 Tt tall; F2 1:2:1 / 3:1; segregation explains dwarf return.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

From his monohybrid crosses Mendel framed two laws: the Law of Dominance and the Law of Segregation.

(i) State the Law of Dominance.
(ii) State the Law of Segregation.
(iii) Which law explains why the F1 are all of one type?
(iv) Which law explains the 3:1 F2 ratio?
questions.answer:
(i) Law of Dominance: when contrasting characters are crossed, only the dominant character appears in the F1; the recessive stays hidden.
(ii) Law of Segregation: the two alleles of a character separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one allele.
(iii) The Law of Dominance explains why the F1 are uniformly of the dominant type.
(iv) The Law of Segregation explains the 3:1 F2 ratio, because the separated alleles recombine to give 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, i.e. 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Mendel crossed pure round-yellow seeded plants (RRYY) with pure wrinkled-green plants (rryy). The F1 were all round-yellow. On selfing the F1, the F2 showed four kinds of seeds.

(i) What is the genotype of the F1?
(ii) Name the four F2 phenotypes and their ratio.
(iii) Which two F2 types are new (recombinant) combinations?
(iv) Which law does this cross demonstrate?
questions.answer:
(i) F1 genotype RrYy (all round-yellow).
(ii) Round-yellow : round-green : wrinkled-yellow : wrinkled-green in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
(iii) Round-green and wrinkled-yellow are the new recombinant combinations not present in the parents.
(iv) The Law of Independent Assortment - each character pair is inherited independently of the other.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Inside the nucleus of a cell are chromosomes made of DNA wound with proteins. DNA is a double helix, and a gene is a segment of DNA. Humans have 46 chromosomes in their body cells.

(i) Where in the cell are chromosomes found?
(ii) What is the shape of the DNA molecule?
(iii) Define a gene.
(iv) How many pairs of chromosomes do humans have, and what are the two types?
questions.answer:
(i) In the nucleus of the cell.
(ii) DNA is shaped like a double helix (a twisted ladder).
(iii) A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a particular character; it is the unit of heredity.
(iv) Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in all): 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Chromosomes in nucleus; DNA double helix; gene = DNA segment; 23 pairs.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In humans, females are XX and males are XY. At fertilisation the egg always carries an X chromosome, while the sperm may carry either X or Y.

(i) Which sex chromosomes does an egg carry?
(ii) Which sex chromosomes can a sperm carry?
(iii) Show how a boy and a girl are produced.
(iv) Who determines the sex of the child, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) An egg always carries an X chromosome.
(ii) A sperm may carry either an X or a Y chromosome.
(iii) X(egg) + X(sperm) -> XX -> girl; X(egg) + Y(sperm) -> XY -> boy.
(iv) The father determines the sex of the child, because it is his sperm that supplies either the X (giving a girl) or the Y (giving a boy); the mother always supplies an X.
questions.explanation: Egg X; sperm X or Y; father decides sex.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive disorder caused by a faulty allele on the X chromosome. A carrier woman (one normal X and one faulty X) marries a normal man.

(i) Why is colour blindness commoner in men?
(ii) What is a carrier?
(iii) Can the daughters of this couple be colour blind? Explain briefly.
(iv) Can the sons be colour blind? Explain briefly.
questions.answer:
(i) Men have only one X chromosome, so a single faulty recessive allele on it is expressed directly (no second X to mask it).
(ii) A carrier is a person (usually a woman) who has one faulty recessive allele but does not show the disorder because her normal allele on the other X masks it; she can still pass the faulty allele on.
(iii) Daughters get one X from the normal father (normal) and one X from the carrier mother (normal or faulty). So a daughter will at most be a carrier, not colour blind (she would need a faulty X from both parents).
(iv) Sons get their single X only from the mother. If they receive her faulty X they will be colour blind; if they receive her normal X they will be normal - about a 50% chance.
questions.explanation: X-linked recessive: sons at risk from carrier mother; daughters carriers.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A farmer notices that some of his wheat plants resist a disease while others die. He saves seeds only from the resistant plants. Over several years his whole crop becomes disease-resistant.

(i) What is the source of the difference among the original plants?
(ii) Is this variation inheritable or acquired?
(iii) How does saving seed from resistant plants change the crop?
(iv) How does this illustrate the role of variation in evolution?
questions.answer:
(i) The difference comes from genetic (inheritable) variation among the plants - some carry alleles giving disease resistance.
(ii) It is inheritable (genetic) variation, because the resistant trait is passed on through the seeds.
(iii) By saving seed only from resistant plants, the farmer selects the resistance alleles; their proportion rises in each generation until the whole crop is resistant.
(iv) It shows that variation provides the raw material and selection (here by the farmer, in nature by the environment) increases useful variations over generations - the basic mechanism behind evolution.
questions.explanation: Genetic variation + selection raises useful traits over generations.
